site_model.what_it_is: A website that turns a written family story and family photos into an illustrated private storybook, with a downloadable PDF and an option to buy a printed hardcover.
site_model.who_it_is_for: Parents and relatives wanting an age-appropriate family story or keepsake featuring their children or other family members.
site_model.value_proposition: Turn a personal family memory into a book that feels personal rather than generic, using family members as the characters.
main_tasks: Sign in or begin a story
Describe the memory and family characters
Obtain a PDF or order a printed hardcover
site_model.pricing_model: New users receive $5 in free credits, with one story generation and preview costing $1 in those credits and no card required. A 30-page Family Storybook is $59, with extra copies costing $35 each. Printed books are described as shipping in five days worldwide.
trust_signals: The site explicitly says no card is needed to start.
It states that photos are never sold, are not used to train public models, and can be deleted.
It says every story is checked against child-safety guidelines.
It openly acknowledges that the company is new and has few reviews.
It says there are no countdown timers or fake sales.
site_model.fit_for_me: It could help me turn my father's kite story into a personal birthday-style keepsake for Oliver, but I would need clear control over the wording and pictures before considering the $59 printed book.

ourlegacy.family/ | Your story becomes a.title: OurLegacy - Turn your family story into a keepsake book
ourlegacy.family/ | Your story becomes a.observation: The OurLegacy home page explains that customers can write a family story, upload photos, and turn the result into a premium keepsake book. It displays prominent calls to action, a $59 Family Storybook price, $5 in free credits with no card required, delivery information, safety claims, and answers to common questions.
ourlegacy.family/ | Your story becomes a.think_aloud: This looks warm and relevant, and the large lettering is easy to read. I appreciate that it says “no card needed” and explains the free credit, but the phrase “Pay per creation” sounds vague, and I would like to be very sure that I will not accidentally spend £59 before I have read and approved the story.

review.purpose: Explain the family storybook service, provide trust and pricing information, and direct visitors to sign in or begin a story.
review.what_is_happening: The page is at its introductory state. A founding-families announcement appears across the top, followed by the main service explanation, a large example image, two ways to begin writing, benefit statements, pricing, safety information, and frequently asked questions.
review.first_impression: The page is warm, attractive, and reasonably easy to read. I like the honest admission that the company is new, although the pricing language could be clearer and the introductory video is not described.

walkthrough.q1_would_try: Yes, I would try beginning my story because the service sounds tailored to turning a real family memory into a keepsake.
walkthrough.q2_notice_control: Yes, I notice the “Sign in” link and the prominent green “Write Your Story” button at the top, as well as “Create Your Storybook” in the main content.
walkthrough.q3_label_matches_goal: Yes. “Write Your Story” clearly describes what I want to do, and I can use “Sign in” because I need to authenticate with my e-mail address.

issues.title: The main video has no text description
issues.why_it_matters_to_me: I cannot tell whether the video is decorative or contains useful information, and I do not want to spend time playing it if it does not explain the process.
issues.fix: Provide a short visible transcript or caption that explains what the video demonstrates, and mark purely decorative video as such.

issues.title: The phrase ‘Pay per creation’ does not make the charge clear
issues.evidence: “Pay per creation — only pay for what you make”
issues.why_it_matters_to_me: This sounds like I might be charged for ordinary writing activities, whereas the detailed answer later says that a new generated draft costs $1 in free credits.
issues.fix: Replace this with wording such as “$5 free to create and preview one story; printed hardcover books start at $59.”

issues.title: The main demonstration appears to feature a family that is not mine
issues.evidence: The large image shows a young girl, and the section says “Your story becomes a book starring your family.”
issues.why_it_matters_to_me: I understand that it is an example, but showing a more representative example or explaining that this is sample artwork would make the relationship to my own family clearer.
issues.fix: Caption the image “Example generated storybook artwork” and include a small example featuring a grandparent and grandchild.

positives: The largest text is clear, high-contrast, and easy for me to read.
The $5 free offer and “no card needed” statement are prominent.
The detailed price of $59 and contents of the 30-page book are stated before I commit.
The site explains photo privacy, child-safety review, and the selected reading age in plain language.
There are several clearly named questions about credits, contents, privacy, character consistency, age suitability, and delivery.
The site admits it is new and does not pretend to have invented reviews.

positives: The page has a simple, uncluttered layout.
The heading and instructions use clear, plain English.
The e-mail field is visibly labelled and marked as required.
Both sign-in methods are clearly separated.
The new-account route is easy to find.

review.purpose: Create a new OurLegacy account so I can begin turning a family memory into an illustrated keepsake.

issues.title: No privacy explanation beside the email field

issues.why_it_matters_to_me: I am willing to provide my email, but I like being told plainly that it will be used for sign-in and relevant account messages.

issues.why_it_matters_to_me: The repeated links make the page slightly busier, although the form itself remains clear.
issues.fix: On the sign-up page, retain the sign-in link within the form and remove the duplicate top-right link.

positives: The page has a clear heading and reassuring explanation of the service.
The form is visually uncluttered and the main controls are easy to see.
Only an email address is requested, rather than a password or payment details.
The email field is clearly labelled rather than relying on the placeholder alone.

ourlegacy.family/auth/signup#/verify-ema.title: OurLegacy - Turn your family story into a keepsake book

ourlegacy.family/auth/signup#/verify-ema.think_aloud: This is clear and orderly, and seeing my email address displayed reassures me that I used the right one. The six code boxes look a little unusual, but the field is labelled properly. I need to check my inbox for the code now.

review.purpose: To confirm that I control the email address before completing account creation.

walkthrough.q1_would_try: Yes, I would check my inbox and enter the code now.
walkthrough.q2_notice_control: Yes, I notice the labelled verification-code textbox and the Continue button.

The main heading and instructions are large and easy to read.
The six individual code boxes give a strong visual indication of the expected code length.
The email address can be edited if I made a mistake.

ourlegacy.family/storybooks | My Storybo.observation: The account has been verified and the site has opened “My Storybooks,” showing an empty collection with a $5.00 credit balance and a prominent “Create Your First Storybook” button.

review.first_impression: The page is uncluttered, the important action is prominent, and it is reassuring to see that there are no storybooks yet because this is my first visit.

walkthrough.q1_would_try: Yes, I want to turn the blue-kite memory into a storybook for Oliver, so I would begin here.
walkthrough.q2_notice_control: Yes, the large teal “Create Your First Storybook” button is immediately visible below the empty-state message.
walkthrough.q3_label_matches_goal: Yes. It says exactly what I want to do, and the surrounding text confirms that family stories will become illustrated memories.

issues.title: Credit balance is not explained on the dashboard

issues.why_it_matters_to_me: On a pension, I want to know at a glance that this is money provided for my use and understand what it can pay for.
issues.fix: Label it “$5.00 free credit” and add a short link, “How credits work,” without opening a separate page automatically.

issues.title: Account menu has no visible label
issues.evidence: [51] is an icon-only button with no accessible or visible label.
issues.why_it_matters_to_me: I should be able to understand what the small symbol in the corner does, especially when checking my account or signing out.

The narrative field is large and its 100–5000 character range is stated.
Uploading a photo is clearly marked “(optional),” giving me control.
The free-credit balance of $5.00 remains visible at the top.

later_issues.title: Clicking Add Character automatically leaves an unexplained blank character card
later_issues.evidence: After using [56] “Add Character”, the page displays Oliver's completed card and a second card labelled only “Character” with “Describe this character...”.
later_issues.why_it_matters_to_me: I cannot tell whether the blank card is ready for another person, a leftover duplicate, or something I must complete before generating.
later_issues.fix: After adding a character, clearly label the new blank card “Describe your second character” and explain that it can be left empty if not needed. Better still, open a focused character-entry panel instead of adding the card immediately.

later_issues.title: The optional photograph language can sound as though it is needed for consistency

later_issues.why_it_matters_to_me: The word “so” suggests photographs guarantee consistency, when descriptions are the alternative and I would prefer not to upload a child's picture.
later_issues.fix: Say, “Add a photo if you wish, or describe each character. Photos may help keep appearances consistent across scenes. Photos are optional.”

later_issues.title: Relationship in the generated story could be incorrect
later_issues.why_it_matters_to_me: This would change who Grandma Maggie is in a personal family keepsake and could make the story confusing for Oliver.
later_issues.fix: Let me edit the description and use the clearly correct wording, “Grandma Maggie, my grandmother” changed to “Grandma Maggie, Oliver's grandmother.”

review.purpose: This page confirms that the submitted family story is being prepared for review and illustration.
review.what_is_happening: The site is analysing the submitted story. Two blank book-page placeholders each show an “Analyzing story...” spinner, and the three-stage indicator shows Review as the current stage. The free-credit balance is now $4.00.
review.first_impression: This is calm and reasonably clear, and the changed balance reassures me that only the agreed $1.00 was used. However, the repeated processing messages give me no sense of how much longer I must wait.

walkthrough.q1_would_try: Yes, but I would wait rather than press anything, since the page clearly says the story is being analysed.
walkthrough.q2_notice_control: There is no action needed at present. I do notice “Go to Create step”, but I would avoid using it while processing.

issues.title: No progress or waiting-time guidance
issues.evidence: The page only says “Analyzing your story...” and “Analyzing story...”, with no percentage, estimated time, or explanation.
issues.why_it_matters_to_me: I do not know whether the work has nearly finished or whether something has gone wrong, and I may keep refreshing unnecessarily.

issues.evidence: “Analyzing your story...” appears under the heading, and “Analyzing story...” appears again in both page placeholders.

positives: The credit balance clearly changed from $5.00 to $4.00, confirming the $1.00 use of free credit.
The three-stage progress indicator makes it clear that Create is complete and the final Output has not yet appeared.
The page is uncluttered and does not demand personal information or payment details while it is working.

later_issues.title: The story has changed the family relationships incorrectly
later_issues.evidence: “One summer, Grandpa’s daddy made something very special” and “Now Grandpa was old — and he had a grandson of his own. His name was Oliver.”
later_issues.why_it_matters_to_me: This is meant to preserve a true family memory. It has confused my father, my daughter, Oliver, and me, so I could not give this book to Oliver as our family story.
later_issues.fix: Preserve the relationships stated in the source: Margaret’s father makes the kite, and years later Margaret, called Grandma Maggie, flies it with her grandson Oliver on the Welsh hill. Do not invent a later character called Grandpa.

later_issues.title: The story introduces an unsupported place jump
later_issues.evidence: “The next day, they went back to Wales!”
later_issues.why_it_matters_to_me: I asked for Oliver to be the hero flying the kite with me on the hill; a sudden journey “back to Wales” and Oliver wearing wellies is not part of the family memory I entered.
later_issues.fix: Keep Oliver and Grandma Maggie together in the original Welsh-hill memory, without inventing travel arrangements or events that were not supplied.

later_issues.title: The story age does not consistently match the requested reading age
later_issues.evidence: “His name was Oliver” and “Many, many years went by. Now Grandpa was old — and he had a grandson of his own.”
later_issues.why_it_matters_to_me: The abstractions and explanation of a family relationship may be difficult for Oliver at five, and the relationship is also wrong.
later_issues.fix: Use short, concrete sentences, simple vocabulary, dialogue and action appropriate for reading age five, while keeping all family relationships accurate.

later_issues.title: Generation status gives no time estimate
later_issues.evidence: “Generating images…” and “0 of 10 scenes complete” with no indication of expected duration.
later_issues.why_it_matters_to_me: Without a time estimate, I do not know whether to wait, refresh, or whether something has gone wrong.
later_issues.fix: Add an approximate wait time and explain whether it is safe to leave the page open.

review.purpose: To review every generated scene, its illustration, and its text before proceeding to the final output.
review.what_is_happening: The completed storybook preview presents ten numbered scenes in sequence. The first two are visible, showing a father and child making a blue kite in a farmhouse and then walking to a windy hill. Further scenes continue below.
review.first_impression: The illustrations are lovely and the words are easy to read, but the story has misunderstood the family relationships at the very beginning. I would be unwilling to give this to Oliver as our family story.

walkthrough.q1_would_try: Yes, I would inspect all ten scenes because I need to know whether the mistakes are occasional or affect the whole book.
walkthrough.q2_notice_control: Yes, the numbered scene headings and the page itself show that there is more content below, although there is no obvious “Next” control.
walkthrough.q3_label_matches_goal: The title “Grandpa's Blue Kite” does not match my intended family memory, which centres on my father making my kite and Oliver later flying it with me.

issues.title: Contradictory generation status
issues.evidence: “Generating images...” appears above “10 of 10 scenes complete” and “100%”.
issues.why_it_matters_to_me: The conflicting message makes me wonder whether the pictures are truly finished or whether the page has failed to update properly.
issues.fix: When generation is complete, replace “Generating images...” with “All images complete” and remove the progress wording.

issues.title: The family relationships have been changed
issues.evidence: Scene 1 says, “Grandpa's daddy made something very special,” and Scene 2 says, “Grandpa and his daddy carried it”.
issues.why_it_matters_to_me: My father made the kite for me; Oliver is my grandson, not a later generation after “Grandpa”. This makes the keepsake factually and emotionally wrong.
issues.fix: Preserve the names and relationships explicitly entered by the user, and require confirmation when generated prose introduces a different relationship or ancestor.

issues.title: The requested characters are missing from the opening memory
issues.evidence: Scene 1 shows “Grandpa's daddy” and a boy, while the requested memory begins with Margaret's father making Margaret's kite.
issues.why_it_matters_to_me: The opening is the heart of my memory, and seeing the wrong people makes the result feel generic rather than personal.
issues.fix: Generate and visually verify Oliver and Grandma Maggie against their entered descriptions, and revise any scene that omits the requested protagonist or changes the event.

issues.title: Unlabelled options give little confidence about what can be changed
issues.evidence: [72]–[81] are buttons labelled only “Options for Scene 1” through “Options for Scene 10”.
issues.why_it_matters_to_me: I need to know whether I can correct the wording, replace an image, or undo a poor scene before proceeding.
issues.fix: Show a clear expanded menu with named actions such as “Edit text,” “Regenerate image,” and “Delete scene,” while making available actions depend on the current step.

issues.title: The title itself is misleading
issues.evidence: The page title is “Grandpa's Blue Kite”.
issues.why_it_matters_to_me: My kite memory is about my father, and I do not want the keepsake branded with a title that implies a different relationship.
issues.fix: Derive the title from the user's intended characters and story, and let me edit it before accepting the output.

positives: The large text and strong contrast are comfortable to read.
The first two watercolour pictures are attractive, warm, and clearly show the kite-making setting.
The numbered scenes make the sequence easy to understand.
The progress bar and exact scene count provide useful structure.
review.abandon_reason: I would consider abandoning if the relationship errors continue throughout, but I need to inspect every scene first.

later_issues.title: The generated character is not the person I described
later_issues.evidence: Scenes 9 and 10 show an elderly silver-haired man with Oliver, while I explicitly described "Grandma Maggie" as having "short silver hair, round glasses, and a blue cardigan." The story also says "Grandpa helped Oliver hold the string."
later_issues.why_it_matters_to_me: This is meant to be a treasured family story for my grandson. An invented grandfather and the absence of Grandma Maggie make it feel like somebody else's book and would be upsetting to give to Oliver.
later_issues.fix: Use the supplied character description and relationship consistently: replace the grandfather throughout with Grandma Maggie, and illustrate her with short silver hair, round glasses, and a blue cardigan.

later_issues.title: Oliver's supplied appearance is not carried into the pictures
later_issues.evidence: The final pictures show a brown-haired child in a red jumper and green trousers; I cannot see the requested freckles, and he is not shown in his green wellies. The final scene also places the kite on the ground rather than giving the picture the requested fly-on-the-hill moment.
later_issues.why_it_matters_to_me: I supplied those details to help produce a recognisable, personal book for a five-year-old, and they are small but meaningful parts of the family memory.
later_issues.fix: Apply the character description to every scene consistently, especially Oliver's brown curly hair, freckles, and green wellies, while retaining a clear, age-appropriate appearance.

inputs.value: The summer my father made me a kite out of an old blue shirt. We carried it up the windy hill behind the old farmhouse in Wales, and the bright blue kite danced high in the sky. My father taught me how to hold the string and how to let out a little more when the wind grew strong. Years later, I told the story to my grandson Oliver. Today we climb the same hill together. Oliver has brown curly hair and freckles, and he is wearing his green wellies. This time Oliver is the hero, and I help him fly Grandpa's blue kite. The kite climbs above the farmhouse and the summer clouds, and Oliver laughs as it swoops and dances. We promise to keep the old blue kite safe and to bring it whenever our family visits Wales.
Oliver, age 5, my grandson and the hero. He has brown curly hair and freckles and loves wearing his green wellies. Make him warm, brave, and full of wonder.

output_reactions.reaction: I can see that a full ten-scene story has been drafted and the layout is calm and readable, but the family story is not accurate enough for a keepsake. My father has been renamed as Grandpa, Oliver has been made his grandson, and an invented trip has replaced my wish to fly with Oliver. I need to inspect the completed illustrations and then correct the narrative.

The first two illustrations are genuinely lovely: the farmhouse feels cosy and the Welsh hill is bright and windy. I also like the clear, short sentences and the gentle rhythm of “Up, up, up.” Yet the story is already wrong about who made the kite and who the people are. The opening shows a man and a boy making it, not my father and me, and the words introduce a “Grandpa” who was never in my memory. I am worried that the polished pictures may conceal major factual mistakes.

The watercolour illustrations are pleasant, warm, and easy for a child to look at, and the kite, Welsh farmhouse, and windy hill provide a coherent setting. The language is also lively and broadly readable. Unfortunately, the essential family relationships are wrong: it invents Grandpa, omits Grandma Maggie altogether, and does not make Oliver the hero of the original kite-flying memory. It feels attractive but not personal enough to keep.

final_summary: Reviewed every one of the ten generated scenes and their illustrations. The output is visually attractive but incorrectly substitutes an invented grandfather for Grandma Maggie and does not preserve Oliver's described appearance, so I would not use it as the keepsake.
